extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, critics, and readers interested in reader-response criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Use Wolfgang Iser's reader-response / reception-theory concepts to evaluate or produce literary texts, focusing on implied reader, narrative gaps, text-reader convergence, and how meaning is realized through reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning as an event between text and reader
rubrics_metrics.description: "Meaning is not an object to be found within a text, but is an event of construction that occurs somewhere between the text and the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate/compose texts on the assumption that meaning is produced in the interaction: the text is a fixed world but the reader realizes meaning by connecting text-structures to their own experience. Example: Iser's constellation metaphor — the 'stars' (textual elements) are fixed but the lines joining them (meaning) vary among readers. Implication for writing: provide stable textual elements while allowing space for readers' constructive activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two poles of a literary work: artistic and aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary work consists of two 'poles': the artistic (the object, the text created by the author) and the aesthetic (the realization accomplished by the reader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both the crafted textual features (language, structure, narrative devices) and the potential/likely realizations they invite in readers. Good texts balance authorial control with openings for aesthetic realization; overly prescriptive texts reduce reader participation, while overly vague texts may fail to constrain interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The implied reader as a network of response-inviting structures
rubrics_metrics.description: The implied reader designates 'a network of response-inviting structures, which impel the reader to grasp the text' and is 'a textual structure anticipating the presence of a recipient without necessarily defining him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, identify how the text encodes an expected reader through viewpoint, knowledge, values, and reading strategies. Consider both aspects Iser names: the reader as textual structure (the standpoint encoded in the text) and the reader as structured act (how a real reader is expected to enact that standpoint). Effective texts craft structures that invite particular responses without fully prescribing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's role as textual structure (vantage points and perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The textual structure refers to the reader’s point-of-view as found within the text; the narrator, characters, plot, and fictitious reader all offer sides of it, and the reader’s vantage point is where they join and converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how narratorial configuration, character perspectives, and embedded fictive readers create a multifaceted vantage point. Good narrative design makes clear (but not exhaustively determined) who the reader is expected to align with and from what angles the story world is presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's role as a structured act (fulfilling textual structures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader’s role as a structured act refers to how a reader fulfills the textual structures by causing them to converge within their imagination; the real reader exists in tension between their historical reality and acceptance of the role offered by the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a text requires readers to activate imagination, infer, and reconcile tensions. Consider the distance between the text's assumed role and likely real readers' backgrounds; effective texts create productive tension rather than alienation. In composition, design prompts and gaps that are fulfillable yet require readerly engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written versus unwritten portions: narrative 'gaps' that invite participation
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary work is composed of both written and unwritten portions; texts produce expectations which are often frustrated, and these interruptions create 'gaps'—the unwritten portions that call for the reader's participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the placement and nature of gaps: they should prompt readers to infer, imagine, or supply connections but remain bounded by the text's interpretive limits. Example: surprises, interrupted flows, and unfulfilled expectations create opportunities for readers to 'fill in' the narrative. Anti-pattern: gaps so large or underdetermined that readers cannot coherently realize the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations, interruptions, and non-arbitrary limits on interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of a text brings about expectations which are interrupted by surprising unfulfillment, producing gaps requiring filling by the reader; these gaps cannot be filled arbitrarily but through interpretive limits given in the text by an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a work, check that the text both leads readers to expect certain continuities and then productively frustrates them, guiding but not dictating interpretation. Composition should provide enough constraint (clues, conventions, contradictions) so reader fillings remain plausible and coherent with the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rereading and retrospective reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: As the reader reflects on what they have read previously, or if they reread the text, new light is shed on happenings within the narrative: 'certain aspects of the text will assume a significance we did not attach to them on a first reading, while others will recede into the background.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a text rewards rereading by enabling shifts in significance and reinterpretation of earlier elements. For writers, embed features (foreshadowing, ambiguity, layered detail) that can be re-evaluated on subsequent readings to enrich interpretive depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of text and reader; breakdown of subject-object division
rubrics_metrics.description: Iser describes the literary work as created when a reader and a text 'converge' and finds the experience to be the breakdown of the subject-object division—in that 'text and reader no longer confront each other as object and subject, but instead the 'division' takes place within the reader himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a text enables an internalized dialogic process within readers where they experience tension/merging between their subjectivity and the text's objectivity. Effective works provoke internal negotiation and personal realization rather than mere external comprehension.
